title: Electromagnetism
seo_title: Secondary 4 Physics: Electromagnetism Worksheets (O-Level 6091 with Answers)
standard_text: Draw the pattern of the magnetic field due to currents in straight wires and in solenoids and state the effect of reversing the current; describe how the magnetic effect of a current is used in a relay and a circuit breaker; describe the force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field and use Fleming's left-hand rule to find its direction; describe the forces between parallel currents; explain the turning effect on a coil and how a d.c. motor works, including the split-ring commutator, and how its speed can be increased (summary of the Singapore-Cambridge O-Level Physics 6091 syllabus).
meta_desc: Free Secondary 4 O-Level Physics worksheets on electromagnetism: magnetic fields of wires and solenoids, electromagnets, relays, Fleming's left-hand rule and the d.c. motor. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: A current makes a magnetic field.
key_sub: Fleming's left-hand rule: field, current, force.
body_html:
How to think about it

An electric current produces a magnetic field.

  • Straight wire: circular field lines; right-hand grip rule (thumb = current, fingers = field). Solenoid: like a bar magnet.
  • Stronger electromagnet: more turns, larger current, soft iron core.
  • Motor effect: a current at right angles to a magnetic field feels a force. Fleming's left-hand rule: First finger Field, seCond finger Current, thuMb Motion.
  • D.C. motor: the split-ring commutator reverses the current every half turn. Faster: more current, stronger magnet, more turns.
Example

Current to the right, field into the page. Force?

left hand: field into page, current right

Answer: up the page

Example

Seen from one end, current flows anticlockwise. Pole?

anticlockwise = N

Answer: north

Common mistakes

  • Using the right hand for the motor effect. Use the left hand.
  • Thinking the commutator changes a.c. into d.c.
  • Forgetting that a wire parallel to the field feels no force.
  • Using steel for the core of an electromagnet.

faq.q: How do you use Fleming's left-hand rule?
faq.a: Hold the thumb, first finger and second finger of your left hand at right angles: first finger = field (N to S), second finger = current (+ to −), thumb = force.

faq.q: How can you make an electromagnet stronger?
faq.a: Increase the current, add more turns of wire, or put a soft iron core inside the coil.

faq.q: What does the commutator in a d.c. motor do?
faq.a: It reverses the direction of the current in the coil every half turn, so the forces keep turning the coil in the same direction.

items.q: What does the split-ring commutator in a d.c. motor do?
c: It reverses the current in the coil every half turn so the coil keeps turning in the same direction.
items.e: The brushes press against it.

items.q: A long straight wire carries a current out of the page. Seen from the front, what is the direction of the magnetic field lines around the wire?
c: straight lines away from the wire
items.e: Right-hand grip rule: thumb along the current, curled fingers give the field direction (out of the page: anticlockwise).

items.q: Two parallel wires carry currents in opposite directions. What happens?
items.e: Their fields push apart between the wires.

items.q: When is there no force on a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field?
c: when the wire is parallel to the field
when the wire is at right angles to the field
items.e: The force is largest at right angles.

items.q: What is produced around a wire carrying a current?
c: a magnetic field along the wire
a magnetic field in circles around the wire
items.e: Shown with iron filings or compasses.

it has no magnetic field at all
items.e: More turns of wire on the coil: stronger.

items.q: What does each finger stand for in Fleming's left-hand rule?
c: First finger: motion; second finger: field; thumb: current
First finger: current; second finger: field; thumb: force
First finger: force; second finger: current; thumb: field
First finger: field; second finger: current; thumb: force (motion)
items.e: FBI: F (thumb), B (first finger), I (second finger).

items.q: What does the magnetic field of a solenoid look like?
c: like the field of a bar magnet, with a uniform field inside
items.e: The ends act as poles.

items.q: How does the magnetic field around a straight wire change further from the wire?
c: It gets weaker: the circles are further apart.
items.e: Field strength falls with distance.

items.q: What are the carbon brushes in a d.c. motor for?
c: to make electrical contact with the rotating commutator
items.e: They allow the coil to turn freely.

items.q: You look at one end of a solenoid. The current flows anticlockwise around this end. What pole is this end?
c: no pole: the field is only inside
items.e: Clockwise current seen from an end makes it a south pole; anticlockwise makes it a north pole.

items.q: You look at one end of a solenoid. The current flows clockwise around this end. What pole is this end?

items.e: Clockwise current seen from an end makes it a south pole; anticlockwise makes it a north pole.

items.q: Two parallel wires carry currents in the same direction. What happens?
items.e: Currents in opposite directions repel.

items.e: Reversing the current: the same strength, but the poles swap.

items.q: A wire carries a current to the right in a magnetic field that points down the page. Use Fleming's left-hand rule. In which direction is the force on the wire?
items.e: Left hand: First finger = Field (down the page), seCond finger = Current (to the right), thuMb = Motion/force (into the page).

items.q: In Fleming's left-hand rule, which finger shows the magnetic field?
items.e: First finger: field. Second finger: current. Thumb: motion.

items.q: A wire in a magnetic field pointing to the left feels a force into the page. Use Fleming's left-hand rule. In which direction is the current?

items.q: In Fleming's left-hand rule, what does the second finger show?

items.q: How does reducing the current change the rotation of a d.c. motor?
